html:
Gross National Happiness is the idea, followed by the government of Bhutan, that a country should judge itself by the wellbeing of its people rather than by its output alone. The phrase is credited to the fourth king, Jigme Singye Wangchuck, who came to the throne in 1972 and said it mattered more than gross domestic product.

It rests on four aims: good government, fair and lasting economic growth, keeping Bhutanese culture alive, and protecting the environment. Bhutan later turned it into a survey based index, and the Constitution of Bhutan of 2008 asks the state to pursue it.

Abroad, the idea fed a wider movement to measure happiness: a United Nations resolution in 2011 and the yearly World Happiness Report. Critics point out that Bhutan stays poor in many ways, and that in the early 1990s it pushed out tens of thousands of Nepali speaking citizens, the Bhutanese refugees, in the name of national culture.
